newsitem.title: JAPAN: INTERVIEW - Japan bank chief welcomes transparency.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Japan bank chief welcomes transparency.

text.p: Greater transparency in Japan's financial markets will help prevent scandals such as the one rocking Dai-Ichi Kangyo Bank Ltd (DKB), the new chairman of a regional bank group said on Wednesday.
Sadaaki Hirasawa said such scandals could be avoided as Japan's financial markets become more transparent in line with the nation's planned "Big Bang" financial reforms.

"As Prime Minister (Ryutaro) Hashimoto says, Japan is creating fair markets... If they (banks) do something against this fairness, the authorities will scrutinise such deeds strictly," said Hirasawa, who is chairman of the 64-member Regional Banks' Association of Japan and also president of the Bank of Yokohama Ltd.
"(Any unfair practices) will be easily seen once the market becomes more transparent."
On Tuesday, prosecutors arrested four former DKB executives on suspicion of violating the Commercial Code with payoffs in the form of illicit loans to a "sokaiya" racketeer.

The scandal, which has now led to the arrests of 14 people, including four other DKB officials and a former Nomura Securities Co Ltd president, is unfolding just as Japan kicks off the "Big Bang" reforms of its long-protected financial sector -- a fact which has made authorities keen to take a tough stance.
Japan is expected to start implementing the Big Bang reforms from the next financial year which starts April 1998.
Hashimoto unveiled the plans last November to catch up with reforms carried out more than a decade ago in Europe and North America.
The regional banks want the reforms to allow them to expand the range of businesses they can be directly involved in, Hirasawa said.

A former Finance Ministry administrative vice minister, Hirasawa, also said that the introduction of the prompt corrective action (PCA) system next April, which gauges the financial health of banks, would help create a fair market.
Under the system, banks must deal with non-performing assets more strictly or risk punishment or being closed down by the authorities.
Hirasawa said the banks in his organisation are set to deal with the financial deregulations because of their strong business ties with regional customers.

Asked if regional banks could lose customers to bigger nationwide commercial banks which are expected to try harder to expand into regional markets, he said: "It depends on how well a bank can meet the requirements of its clients. Regional banks have well-established relationships with local businesses and are linked up with local interests."
